faqs.a: Keyword density is the percentage of times a keyword appears relative to the total word count. For 'cat' appearing twice in 9 words, density = (2 / 9) x 100 = 22.22%.

There is no official Google percentage — Google's own guidance is that the text should 'sound natural'. As a rule of thumb, 1–2% for a primary keyword in a long article is comfortable; anything above 3–4% starts to look forced to readers.
faqs.q: What is a good keyword density?

faqs.a: Counting matches case-insensitively on whole words. 'Cat', 'CAT', and 'cat' all count; 'cats' or 'concatenate' do not, because the match uses word boundaries.
faqs.q: Is the keyword match case-sensitive? Does 'cats' count for 'cat'?

faqs.a: Yes. The top-10 table excludes common English stopwords (the, and, is...) so real content words surface. Phrases skip pairs where both words are stopwords.
faqs.q: Why do the top-words and top-phrases tables exclude some words?

faqs.a: Your text is processed in memory in your browser and never sent anywhere. Nothing is stored or logged.
Punctuation is stripped and words are split on whitespace, so 'well-known' counts as one token and 'don't' counts as one token. Numbers count as words.
faqs.q: How are hyphenated words and numbers counted?

keyword-density-checker.formula:
Density (%) = (keyword occurrences / total words) x 100
Word count = tokens after lowercasing and stripping punctuation
Keyword match = case-insensitive, whole-word (word boundaries)
Phrase density (%) = (phrase occurrences / (total words - 1)) x 100
howTo: Paste your article, product description, or paragraph into the text box.
Type the keyword or phrase you want to check in the keyword field.
Read the density percentage, occurrence count, and totals instantly.
Scan the top-10 words and top-5 phrases tables for accidental overuse.
Rewrite the overused spots and re-paste until the density reads naturally.
keyFacts: Keyword density = (keyword occurrences / total words) x 100. A density of 2% means the keyword appears twice per 100 words.
Matching is case-insensitive and whole-word: 'Cat' counts for 'cat', but 'cats' does not.
The top-10 single-word table filters out common English stopwords so content words surface.
The top-5 two-word phrases table skips pairs where both words are stopwords.
Google has no official density rule — its published test is simply that the text should sound natural.

keyword-density-checker.workedExample: Take the sentence 'The cat sat on the mat. The cat slept.' and the keyword 'cat'. Tokenizing gives 9 words: the, cat, sat, on, the, mat, the, cat, slept. The keyword 'cat' appears twice (case-insensitive, whole-word), so density = (2 / 9) x 100 = 22.22%. Removing stopwords (the, on) leaves cat x2, sat x1, mat x1, slept x1 — the top-words table. For two-word phrases there are 8 possible pairs; 'the cat' occurs twice, so its phrase density = (2 / 8) x 100 = 25.00%, the highest in the table. A 22% density on a real article would signal heavy overuse.
